utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. Please be seated. Mr. Riedlmayer, you'll first be examined by Mr. Traldi. You find him to your right. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name and occupation for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: My name is Andras Janos Riedlmayer I'm an art documentation specialist employed by Harvard University.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how long have you worked as Harvard?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm about to complete 28 years of service next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 28813.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is this the curriculum vitae that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does it correctly set out your experience and your current position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28813 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28813 receives P2504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you briefly describe the research work you've done into cultural property during the period of war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I started looking into damage to cultural property in the former Yugoslavia while the war was still going on, collecting publicly available documentation. I wrote about it and in the mid-1990s I also helped organise cultural reconstruction initiatives. In 1999 after the end of the Kosovo war, I conducted a field survey in Kosovo with a colleague, an architect, with the results submitted to both UNMIK, the UN administration in Kosovo and to the UN war crimes Tribunal. Subsequently I was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to also prepare reports on Bosnia. These were based initially on a field survey conducted in the summer of 2002 and then also on subsequent visits to Bosnia and on documentation that I have collected over the past decade and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And had you been familiar with the culture of the Balkan region before you did the work you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I received my undergraduate degree in history from the University of Chicago in 1969 and wrote my senior thesis on the subject of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Congress of Berlin. I received a graduate degree in Near Eastern studies basically in Ottoman history from Princeton University and there too part of my research had to do with the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you also speak what we refer to as B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I speak it with an accent but I can read it quite fluently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When did you begin to acquire your familiarity with the language?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In the early 1990s I took a course at Harvard and I've been working at it ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you briefly summarise for the Chamber what you view as included within the ambit of cultural heritage in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Cultural heritage consists of all the cultural production, obviously, of the peoples of the former Yugoslavia, but the cultural heritage that I've documented for the Tribunal is limited to immovable cultural heritage, meaning buildings, institutions, rather than works of art or other things that are considered movable cultural heritage. These typically consist of historic landmarks, buildings, monuments, as well as houses of worship of the various religious communities and archives and libraries as institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Based on your studies and your work, can you tell us about the role of houses of worship in Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat cultures?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Houses of worship in neighbourhoods and villages were often the centres of religious life and, to some extent, also of cultural and social life and they symbolised the visible presence of a community in a given place. So Mahala quarter of a city or a village would be immediately recognisable as a place where Muslims or Croats lived by the presence of a minaret or a church steeple. Many of these neighbourhoods and villages had a mixed population, and in that case you would see each groups' prominent religious monument visible in the landscape. In the late 20th century especially in urban areas the majority of the population was not particularly religiously observant. They might go to a mosque or a church mainly for the big transition of life events such as weddings or funerals. Nevertheless, the presence of these constituted the sign that this community to which they belonged had history in that place and belonged there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also discuss just now as well as in paragraphs 60 to 64 of your report some other cultural sites, religious archives, libraries, a monastery. Can you explain the importance of those types of sites for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, as in much of south-eastern Europe, the civil registration of births, deaths, and marriages came along relatively late in history, basically around World War I, as a result of which the parish archives and the archives of the Islamic religious councils in each community held not only the records that pertained to the operation of those religious communities, but also the history of entire families and of entire groups of people. In other words, their destruction is a loss not only to the operation of a parish but also to the whole group whose past is captured in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn briefly to your current employment. You described yourself as an art documentation specialist. Can you be more specific about the position that you hold?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I direct the documentation centre of the Aga Khan programme for Islamic architecture at Harvard university. The Aga Khan programme is a joint programme between the school of architecture at MIT and the art history department and urban planning department at Harvard. The documentation centre actively collects documentation on Islamic architecture from around the world in all formats, including photographs, digital images, textual documentation. We also create some of our own documentation by conducting photography missions. We typically send out groups of students on summer projects under supervision to bring back documentation of specific sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as director of the documentation centre, do you -- are you involved in deciding what documentation becomes part of the collection?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We -- for many years I have served on committees that approve student projects for summer documentation and when they bring back the documentation I oversee the selection of what gets kept and what does not, what makes good documentation and what is not worth keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you make similar evaluations of what made for suitable documentation in the course of preparing your report for this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Definitely. Let's consider, for example, a building. Documentation would typically consist of a before and after picture. If you have an after picture, it has to be one that provides sufficient information about the building to tell what happened to it. In many cases we also -- I mean, I also was able to obtain cadastral plans or pre-war ground plans. This was very useful, especially in cases where the building had been totally destroyed. It was then a task to compare the site in its post-war condition with the pre-war plan and match things up. So that is one aspect. Another aspect is textual documentation. Both in advance of my field of war and afterwards I would collect every possible published documentation on particular sites, including published photos, descriptions, histories, and so forth. And I would evaluate these sources as to their reliability and the utility for the purpose and then match them up with the visual documentation in order to come to an evaluation of what happened, both to specific sites and to a pattern of sites at a larger scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Both in your work at the documentation centre and in preparing the report, do you visit habitually every cultural site you're researching?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No, I do not. Typically in my work in the documentation centre, I work with photographs, texts, and digital images, and only when I go out on the very occasional field trip do I actually collect and create the documentation. In my fieldwork for the Tribunal, I've been able on average to visit about half the sites that I documented. I should also like to add that of -- in the process of evaluating the information for sites which I have not visited, I often compare what that particular source has to say about the sites which I did visit, and thereby be able to judge how reliable its descriptions or its evidence is for what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for sources that you used regularly, your observations about those sources' reliability is -- are set out in appendix 1 to your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would ask that the Court Officer call up MFI P2503. And I believe what we have is 2504. It should be 65 ter 28815.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this the first page of the expert report you drafted for this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can you describe any additional information to what you've said already that the Chamber should have in understanding the approach you took to preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Could you clarify what you mean? Methodology or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just -- just briefly any additional steps you took beyond the fieldwork and sources you looked at above, anything that's important for a reader to understand the process of preparation.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the process of preparation includes, first of all, looking at published and unpublished allegations of destruction, also researching what buildings and institutions existed prior to the war. Then, in accordance with the terms of reference set by my mission which specified which municipalities I should collect information on, then assembling all possible documentation both from sites that I covered in my various visits to Bosnia and sites for which I have documentation. If there are sites for which there is insufficient documentation, I tried to obtain additional documentation wherever possible; if that was not possible, I had criteria by which I determined what the threshold was below which I would simply not cover a site. As I set out in my description of my methodology, that typically included sites for which there was no photo documentation available. Photographs were required in large part because damaged descriptions in the public -- published documentation, such as that issued by the religious communities, was not always very precise or reliable. If a site is described as completely devastated, what does that mean? In the absence of either a site visit or good photographs, I had no way of knowing what had really happened to a site like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss two specific points within the report at this juncture. First, in paragraphs 18 and 19 you describe which sites were included. Were you able -- sorry, did you exclude from the ambit of the report any sites which you were able to prove to the thresholds you'd just described had existed before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No. I included everything for which adequate documentation was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regardless of whether anything had happened to it during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 15 you describe your report as documenting cases of "deliberate destruction." What steps did you take to identify destruction as deliberate?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all, one of my concerns was to ascertain whether a building still stood on the eve of the war. There was at least one site in the schedule D list, which I determined had been damaged before the war. There was another site which apparently was essentially a site that hadn't existed. It was a duplicate name for another mosque, this is Kutina. So that was the first step. The second one is how do you know it's deliberate? Okay. You look at a building, first of all, if it is falling down simply due to neglect, then you know that is not necessarily deliberate damage. Then you look at the context, is the building more damaged or less damaged than surrounding buildings, assuming they're -- it is in a context where there are surrounding buildings. And I include some statistics, I believe, in footnotes 17 and 27, where I compiled this information and found, in fact, that in the majority of cases where this information was available, the surrounding buildings had been less damaged and that these particular buildings had, indeed, been the focus of damage. So that I would call deliberate damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 28816, page 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As that comes up, sir, aside from the report, did you also produce specific records called formatted entries for each of the sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. My report consists of three parts. One is the database which we'll talk about more later. That covers every site in these municipalities for which I have sufficient information. The second one is the text report which we have already discussed. And the third one is the formatted entries. The formatted entries, so-called, cover each of the schedule D indictment sites plus Srebrenica. Formatted entry is simply an expanded version of the database entry. For technical reasons, database entries can only accommodate a limited amount of information, two vertical photos, two horizontal photos, and a limited amount of text. For most of these sites I had more information than that available and so I put them into essentially PDF document. So sites might have additional photos, additional text and the formatted entry reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is this that we're seeing here an example of those formatted entries?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the mosques in Rogatica, the town of Rogatica, it is the Arnaudija mosque and it is a site that I'd visited personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation, please, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, page 70, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the relationship between the three photographs on this page?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The two photos at the bottom are pre-war photographs of the mosque. The photo on top shows how it looked in the period after the war. I visited the site in 2002. This photo is from 2005 from the Centre for Islamic Architecture of the Islamic Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I chose it rather than my photo because my photo was a poor exposure. It was getting dark when I was there. As you can see, the site of the mosque is empty. The building is simply gone. In the background at right is a building which is an updated version of the buildings you see in the two pre-war photos, a bus station. So it confirms that we're looking at the same site. When I visited the site, I could also see disturbances in the ground cover. I was there in the summer. This photo is from the autumn, so the ground is covered with leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In cases where mosque sites had become empty, like the photograph we see here, were there characteristic features which you looked for to determine that a mosque had at one point stood there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There were several things that one could do to determine that a building had stood there. One I just alluded to is the disturbance in the ground. This is most frequently reflected by the fact that when you tear down a building, typically if the foundations are not removed the growth of vegetation will be different on top of what used to be stone and on top of undisturbed earth. And so very often you can trace the outlines of a building even if the building has gone because the grass and weeds will be very sparse or stunted where walls had stood and much more lush where walls hadn't stood. So you can pace it. One can match these up to pre-war plans. Also if one has pre-war photos it is often possible to match up the context, either by adjacent buildings or by topography. Sometimes there are outlines of hills that you can match up, so the background tells you something. There are roads. And finally, if one has plans, many of these mosques had very specific dimensions and I would measure. There are also other ways you can tell. The sites of destroyed mosques often leave behind the Linden tree that is traditionally planted next to the mosque when it's dedicated in Bosnia. Linden is going back to pagan times, where a sacred tree of the Slavs -- and it was customary, still is, in Bosnia that when a new mosque is erected that to the right of the entrance a Linden tree is planted. The Bosnian term is Lipa. And so often you would find a Linden tree and you would find a disturbed ground and the other thing we would often we would find is a large deposit of garbage marking where the mosque stood. Often these sites seemed to be deliberately chosen for the deposit of garbage and which seemed very strange because often this was in the middle of a settlement so not exactly the place where you would expect smelly refuse to be stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding this specific mosque, Arnaudija, Your Honours, I would refer you to adjudicated fact 1137 and the evidence of RM081.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, now I'm going to turn to the database. The database is not compatible with e-court so to assist in understanding its functioning I would ask Ms. Stewart to pull up an example and if we could play it in Sanction. The example we're looking at here is the Kukavica mosque in Foca. Do you see it on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this a site you visited yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe what we're seeing in the pictures on this page?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So, first of all, you will note the structure of the database entry, where there are different forms of the name of the building in English and in B/C/S, its precise location including GPS, its date of construction, whether or not it was a listed monument, meaning under legal protection as a historical landmark, and then its function, and finally the context, whether it was heavily damaged or lightly damaged, and what the surrounding buildings look like. The pictures you see include pictures I've taken of the exterior of the mosque. One facade of the mosque has collapsed. On the picture at bottom right you can see the place where the minaret stood before it was destroyed. There's a pre-war photo that shows the context and there's also a shot taken of the interior in June of 1996 right after the war by a journalism student who -- whom I asked to take it. He did charity work in Bosnia the summer after the war and you can see that the interior is filled with rubbish and a pig skull. Above the pictures is my technical description exactly of what the damage is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to point to us which one is the interior with the pig skull.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's the second photo from the top. It's the only one that doesn't show the exterior of the building and the pig skull in the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to zoom in on that or is that impossible?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll defer to Ms. Stewart on that, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- but if we get a second, we'll try.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it is -- is this just an image or -- oh, here it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- Mr. Riedlmayer, could you assist us by -- you see that there's an -- there's an arrow at -- to guide it to where we find the pig skull. I think at this moment we are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's at the very centre of the image. You can see the eye hole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I see it. Could we just -- so that we are sure you are looking at the same, could I ask the person who's handling the arrow to go to the picture and then to -- I think that is where it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we all agree it's in the very centre, you see a hole where the eye would have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the mouth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the right side of the mouth. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, why did you choose to provide the database along with the formatted records?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The database is a database that I designed using the FileMaker software which allows one to search and sort on all fields. It is very useful, I believe, for deriving statistical information. One can search, for example, by municipality, by degree of destruction, by type of building, by context, and so forth. So most of this statistical information that you find in my report was generated by searches of the database. And I thought it was -- would be useful for the Court to have the database as a whole to be able to do searches of Their Honours' advising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put at this moment another additional question. How did you establish that the skull was the skull of a pig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a good question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, could you please remain -- if you want to consult with counsel, you're -- you have to remain seated -- Mr. Mladic, you have to remain seated and if you want to consult briefly and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Harvard has a museum of comparative zoology. I took the photo over to the museum of comparative zoology where they have a collection of animal skulls and I compared them and I consulted the curator, and it was a positive identification that it is a pig skull. It is also compatible with information on other sites, though not this particular one, that talks about pig skulls being -- pigs' heads being deposited at sites of mosques because, as you're probably aware, pigs are considered unclean by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one other question of detail. The description of the photograph says "skulls" and you talked about a skull.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a -- do we miss something or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is a typographical error. There's one skull. There are other bones that you can see amidst the rubbish. The interior of the mosque was burned out and this is how it was given to me by the student who took the photograph and he described it as skulls so I just wrote it. But the one I could identify was the one right in the middle of the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a largish building, so there may have been other ones outside of the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether it's a typo or not is unclear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's unclear in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But in any case, there is at least one identifiable one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, I understand you have three brief corrections regarding the database which I'm simply going to read to you now. First, the cover page of the database does not mention Srebrenica. Does the database also include Srebrenica sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, regarding the Catholic church in Kozaric the database entry lists it as damaged in June 1999. Should that date read June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, and that is a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And finally, the Catholic church in Cesina, Sanski Most, is it correct that that church was destroyed in June of 1993 rather than in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is my information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that correction should also apply, should it not, to paragraph 59 of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask the Court Officer to call up 65 ter 28814.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we see it already on the right. Can you tell the Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it's an appendix that I devised called principal elements of a Bosnian mosque. I put it together in order to aid the Court in understanding my database in which I refer to these terms and it -- if you had this guide, you would understand, first of all, what is said without it needing to be explained. But also this explains the relative position of elements of the mosque to each other. Every mosque in Bosnia is oriented towards Mecca, which in Bosnia is generally a south-easterly direction. And almost all mosques have the minaret to the right of the entrance. The other elements are laid out there. There's a prayer hall. There is a prayer niche called the mihrab marked with the letter D. That indicates the direction of the prayer. To the right of the prayer niche is a pulpit called a mimber from which sermons are delivered. The minarets typically have an internal staircase and that is where the muezzin, the man who gives the prayer call, goes up the minaret. If we could have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So on this one -- should I wait for the second one? Yes. On this one you can see the exterior of the same mosque before the war. So you can see that three-quarters of the way up the minaret is a balcony from which the prayer call is issued. The balcony is called a "serefe" and it is important to note its presence because in mosques that have been ruined you often have that as an element among the damaged masonry. The front of most mosques has a portico here marked with a letter B, it comes in various shapes, but it is again a distinctive element of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you use here the example of the Aladza mosque in Foca. Why did you choose that example?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Basically because I had good documentation for it. It was a particularly notable document and there are books about it, and so it was easy to choose photos that were clear and understandable and I was able to locate good floor plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you studied what happened to that mosque, what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The mosque was completely destroyed in 1992 and its ruins were razed and it was one of those sites where all you could see was the outlines of foundations after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have please 65 ter 28816, page 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what site do we see here on this page?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This is from the formatted entry for the Aladza mosque. On the top photo which was taken in June of 1996 by the same student who took the picture of the interior of the Kukavica mosque. You can see the circular outline in the front is of the ablution fountain in front of the mosque and then behind it you can see the outlines of the foundations and some buildings in the background, including some that have suffered damage. It's the Imam's house between the trees. The photo below is this site as it looked some years later, with more of a growth of vegetation, but you can still see, if you look carefully, the places where there had been a foundation of a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 142 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what site are we seeing here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This is also in the town of Foca. This is next to the iron bridge on the Drina River. In September of 2004, there was an exhumation of a suspected mass grave site. As far as I know, no human remains were found, but at the depth of 7 metres, identifiable fragments of the Aladza mosque were found, column capitals, carved stone work, pieces of the mihrab were recovered from beneath tonnes of refuse. This was at some considerable distance from where the mosque had stood, so the rubble had been moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 30376. While that comes up, Your Honours, regarding the mosques in Foca I would refer you also to adjudicated fact 721 and transcript page 17666. This, I'm afraid, is just a surrogate sheet. Ms. Stewart will play what I'm looking for in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this spreadsheet, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a spreadsheet I put together at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor. It covers all of the reports I did for the six Bosnia-related cases at this Tribunal, and it's simply a compilation of each of the sites that were surveyed. There are -- I don't remember the exact figure, but it was something like 535 sites. I have -- yes. And the red entries are Islamic religious sites, the blue entries are Catholic religious sites, and there's a handful of black entries which are heritage sites which are not connected to a particular community, such as the oriental institute in Sarajevo, for example, which was a state institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In studying those more than --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Those are in black.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In studying those more than 500 sites, can you tell the Chamber what patterns, if any, you were able to discern in the relationship between the location of a site and what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again, would you clarify what you mean by the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. Two of the pieces of information on this spreadsheet are where in Bosnia a specific site is located and the level of damage associated with that site.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. What is indicated on these is, first of all, which municipality they're in, and then for each there is a GPS location, the degree of damage, and the date if it can be established. And the general pattern was that sites which had been in territory which at various points in the war was under the control Bosnian Serb forces tended to be heavily damaged or destroyed. Sites that were near the confrontation lines would have lesser degrees of damage, typically damage category 2. And sites which were undamaged would be inside territory that was controlled by the Bosnian government forces for the duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were those patterns consistent across all the municipalities you've studied?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does this spreadsheet include every site in those municipalities for which you determined you had sufficient documentation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it might be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break, but before we take the break could we just have a bit of a closer look to the spreadsheet because we see now columns A, B, C, D, and E, but what then follows and what was apparently referred to is not visible. Could we just move to F, G, and H so that we -- yes, so that we have an -- F is the condition of damage, I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And G is the reported date of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be totally clear, perhaps the number in column F, does that correspond to the scale you set out in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We've seen it. We take a break. Mr. Traldi, will you be able to set up everything during the break or would we need another five minutes after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the break should be sufficient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Approximately, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I asked for the electronic version of 65 ter 13413, but having looked at it, if you zoom in then it turns out that the -- how do you say it, the number of pixels, et cetera, is insufficient to even read it when zoomed in. I don't know how you are going to deal with that or whether you'd expect us to take home one of these huge maps. We have to find a way that we cannot only look at it in this courtroom but also later if we have to deliberate on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can explore the technological side of things. The map itself is in custody of court management, and so we'll try and work things out with them as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we have a way to access that material and be able to read what is written on it as well. We take a break but not until after Mr. Riedlmayer has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before we start with the map, sir, I know we'd arranged a pointer with Registry. Have you been provided with it? I'll take that as a yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then do you recognise the map that's just to your left?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map compiled by Mr. Bekir Besic, who was a member of the Council of Islamic Community of Banja Luka, and who now lives as a refugee in a third country. He mapped the sites of destroyed mosques based largely on the published report by Muharem Omerdic, which is cited among the sources of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this also one of the sources you used in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It is not a -- the Omerdic or the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The map.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The map is provided largely as an illustration of the pattern of destruction, but insofar as my report is based on specific subsets of municipalities, obviously I was not dealing with the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So can you tell us, to start working with it, just generally what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So what we're looking at is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The large green circles reflect the larger towns. At the centre is Sarajevo. In the south is Mostar. Here are Travnik and Zenica at the centre, Banja Luka at the top, and Tuzla in the east. This is -- in the far east is Gorazde in the Drina valley. The various coloured dots on the map represent damaged, destroyed, and intact mosques. I'm sorry that it's so far from the Bench, but maybe the camera can zoom in. I also know from having handled the map that it does fold and can be spread out on a table. So it should be possible to handle it outside of a court setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can you just let us know what respectively the red, yellow, and green dots represent.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Red dots marked the sites of destroyed or severely damaged mosques, yellow dots mark mosques that are lightly damaged, and green dots mark the sites of mosques that are undamaged. These are not in complete match with my multi-point scale, but I think it's generally consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And geographically, how does the distribution of these sites relate to the pattern that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think it matches the phenomenon I described with reference to the Excel spreadsheet that we discussed shortly before the break. You can see, Your Honours, the pattern of red dots. If you start here in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see red dots going down to Mostar and then in the other direction up this way --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is difficult to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope you could hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can hear you. The interpreters cannot hear you if you move away from your microphone, and therefore then there'll be no translation in other languages. So if you could -- is there any way to have an extended microphone fitted or is there -- that's not possible. Then I have to ask that the map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- will be moved slightly and that you stay as close to the microphone, and if you speak that the microphone is adjusted in such a way that if you then would speak slowly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask transcriber and interpreters to immediately yell at me, either directly or through my earphones, that they cannot follow you. And could I really invite you to slow down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that we -- I can intervene whenever there's a need to do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps if you could, you were describing specific regions where there are particular concentrations of red dots. Perhaps if you could indicate for the Chamber, whilst sitting, there's this specific region where there's a particular concentration and then point, that would be easiest for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. So what I was trying to point out is that the pattern which I indicated with reference to the GPS spreadsheet is graphically illustrated on this map. The red dots are concentrated pretty much in territory that was under the control of Bosnian Serb forces at various points during the war. This is the case for the following regions: In Southern Herzegovina, in Eastern Bosnia, up the Drina valley, and then across Northern Bosnia, and then down towards Kupres and Donji Vakuf. Yellow dots tend to follow the confrontation lines during the war. The only place where yellow dots appear elsewhere in some profusion is in Central Bosnia, which was the site of the war within the war that pitted Croat militias against the forces aligned with the Sarajevo government. None of the municipalities in this case are located in Central Bosnia so it's not of direct relevance I don't think. The green dots which indicate the locations of intact mosques are concentrated in areas which were under the control of the Sarajevo government throughout the war. For example, up here in what was the Bihac pocket in the far north-western corner of Bosnia and over here in the central zone near Zenica and near Tuzla. And you will observe, Your Honours, no green dots in any of the territories that were under the control of the VRS during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to approximate for the Chamber the number of red dots on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There is a statistic on the map. It adds up to 900-odd red dots, in other words, severely damaged or destroyed mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of those 900 or so red dots, about how many have you visited yourself, how many of those sites over the years?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think roughly half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And are you able to approximate what percentage of the total mosques on the map are represented with those red dots?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, roughly three-quarters of the mosques represented on the map have been either damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the questions I have about the map. I put on the record earlier, I think, the 65 ter number but just to be completely clear 13413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's 13413. I have one additional question. Could you again tell us where the concentration of green dots are found because I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will stand up and simply point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I have a look at the map which is before us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is one group around Bihac in north-western Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's another group in Central Bosnia, east and north-east of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there's a third group that's in the Tuzla region, north of Tuzla, and slightly east and south of Tuzla. Everywhere else you either see yellow dots, such as along here, along the front lines or -- or you see red dots which are pretty much everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer, for that. Mr. Traldi, you have done with the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so we can -- the map perhaps can be moved away so that the public gallery has a better view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it's being moved, sir, the larger green circles, what do those represent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that they represent the larger population centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I'd ask that 65 ter 30375 be called to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document I prepared at the request of OTP, just at the end of last month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What is -- what does it record?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It records information in -- that I received from informants during the course of my fieldwork as to who is allegedly the party responsible for the destruction of various buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you were preparing this chart, where did you locate the information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I -- all the information is derived from my previous reports that were submitted to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we next have Exhibit P178.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to be very quick about this. Did you review the maps for the following municipalities that are contained in this book: Foca, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, Novi Grad, and Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you confirm that with one exception the mosques and churches represented there were located correctly based on your research?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is that exception that your research indicates that the mosques at Pudin Han and Velagici were in fact the same mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we next have 65 ter 03120.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I am familiar with it. I received a copy from the Islamic Community, the Medzlis of the Islamic Community in Kljuc during my fieldwork and a copy was also provided to me by OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The sites in this document that you were familiar with, were they described correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that sometimes the Islamic or Catholic community wouldn't when they prepared a document like this use the most scientific terminology in describing the consequences. Does that caveat apply here as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and it's worth noting that the damage described is encyclopedic; in other words, they include not only events of the 1992-1995 war, but they also catalogue destruction from World War II but they make it clear which is which.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The document assigns financial values to the consequences for each site. Do you have any comment on the value of these sites for that community?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think the -- I looked very closely at instance. I've worked on a couple of reconstruction projects after the war. I have some sense of what it really takes to reconstruct a historic building and the values they assign here are very much the per square metre values that are used for calculating costs of housing reconstruction. So, in financial terms, this is a very low statement. The real value is what I was trying to point out before the break, namely, the symbolic value for these communities of what these mosques represented, both in terms of their being sacred sites and what they embodied for the community, symbolically and functionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Relatedly, in paragraphs 43 to 45 of your report you discuss the impact of the destruction of houses of worship on the communities which prayed there. And you refer to quotes from a Serb leader from Sokolac and a Muslim resident of Banja Luka. Why did you choose to include those quotes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think precisely with a view of assisting the Court in determining what was the reason for the destruction of these mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in terms of discussions that you're familiar with from people in Bosnia, are those quotes an exhaustive list of statements you're familiar on the topic or illustrative?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: They're meant to be illustrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd refer Your Honours as well to transcript page 17388. And at this point I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to pull up in Sanction the slide show that we've prepared and we'll go through this in I would expect 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what we're looking at in this first picture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It's one of the pictures from my formatted entry. It's the mosque in Vrhpolje, a village in Sanski Most municipality. This is a picture taken in December of 1995 at the very end of the war. You can see to the left the burned-out houses of the village. In the centre is the mosque, the mosque at that point was still under construction. There is a stump of the minaret up front with a pile of rubble covered by snow, and the mosque itself, as it has no windows and holes in the wall. I would call it a lightly damaged mosque because it is not structurally impaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it was relatively rare the mosques you identified were lightly damaged. Is it surprising to find this mosque lightly damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Not as such. The -- if Your Honours refer to my report, you will see that mosques that were lightly damaged, I believe there were only six of them, for the most part were mosques that had not yet been formally inaugurated. They were under construction. At some cases they had been in informal use as overflow areas for holiday prayers, but basically they had not been registered with the civil authorities as active mosques yet, they hadn't been inaugurated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What did you take from that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: My contention is that given that very often in close vicinity to these unfinished mosque, older mosques had been destroyed, that there must have been some sort of list which excluded these buildings. If one considers that during the war things like explosives, manpower, transportation were all in high demand, I can -- it's a reasonable conclusion to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Riedlmayer, you say at page 35, line 25, that you -- the mosques that were lightly damaged you believe had not been inaugurated and you believe there were only six of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were mosques, Your Honour, that were under construction on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The six referred -- the six number refers to those that were under construction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, because the transcript was saying that those that you -- that were slightly damaged and I was just going to ask that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- how do you reconcile that with the yellow dots but you have answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm sorry for interrupting. If we just can get a number of the document, which number is the document we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The slide show's prepared using images in the formatted entries, and so, for instance, this one, the formatted entry for Vrhpolje, appears on page 109 of 65 ter 28816. I'm told that the slide show has been assigned 65 ter 30417 and can be viewed separately that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would add also that the number before Vrhpolje and on each of these slides refers to the number of the formatted entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to return briefly to the question His Honour Judge Moloto asked you, and when you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This 30417 is not on the list so for us it is really hard to follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is created like a clip from a video that is on the list. This is essentially clips from the formatted entries. Each of these images is taken from a page of 65 ter 28816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does this assist you? If Mr. Lukic would need more time do you know from what pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For each slide, Your Honour, I can put on the record where that site's entry begins. So the Vrhpolje entry begins at page 169 of 28816. And I'll do that as I start each new site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If that's useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that you can find it on the relevant page, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There is also the database, of course, which is searchable by the name of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I'd like to go back, sir, to Judge Moloto's question, if I might. And he asked you about the number of lightly damaged sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I believe, in your report, you referred to six lightly damaged sites --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- and you discuss each of them individually?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, that's a different number than the number of yellow dots on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The yellow dots on the map cover all of Bosnia and they're concentrated mostly in municipalities that were on the front line, like near Doboj in the Posavina corridor. The fact that there are so few of them in the municipalities covered by this report is simply due to the choice of indictment municipalities. So the two numbers represent different basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is still the same site.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a photo taken in the first summer after the war, summer of 1996. And I've included it just to show a close-up of what really happened to this minaret. The minaret had been finished before the war and you can see there's only a massive stump left. The way one can tell that it was destroyed is you can see hanging down from the minaret strips of masonry connected by the iron rod within. This is a modern construction method where originally you had the rebar, the iron bars, connected to the concrete structure and cladding. And in the way that I described in the report, explosives were placed inside the stairwell and the force blew it out. I believe we can see it more clearly on the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we go to the next then. And, Mr. Lukic, this is the Sanica mosque in Kljuc and begins at page 173 of 28816.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is another mosque, it was a mosque that was heavily damaged. My damage categories apply here to the extent not only was the minaret damaged but the mosque itself is completely burned out, it's lost its roof, the walls are deteriorated. But here you can see very clearly the phenomenon I was referring to, the strips hanging down from the minaret. They had been forced apart by the force of the blast, and so the iron bars were bent out very much like a wilted flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding events in Sanica I would refer you to the evidence of RM10 and 21. If we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This slide refers to the Kotor Varos church. In 65 ter 28816 it begins on page 191.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This is a photograph that I took during my field visit. It's the interior of the church of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Kotor Varos, it's the main parish church, and you can see that the church is completely burned out. I was able to ascertain the fact that it was burned out by the fact that wooden elements, such as the cross on the wall behind what used to be the altar were completely charred. Not visible in this photo but behind where I was standing there were Serbian graffiti on the walls, the roof was missing, and the two steeples of the church had been blown up and one of them had fallen into the parish house which was next to the church. So this I would call a heavily damaged building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would refer you to adjudicated fact 818. And then ask that we turn to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This -- the formatted entry for the Hanifici mosque begins on page 183 of 28816.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the mosque in Hanifici, in Kotor Varos municipality. It is a photo taken by an OTP investigator in 2001, and it shows the entrance facade of the mosque, so one is looking from the north-west towards the south-east. You can tell that first of all that it is a burned-out building because you can see the charred roof structure. At the time I was there, I went inside and also took photos of the other side of the building which had soot marks on it. And to the right of the entrance is the stump of the minaret. You can see it. It is broken off at an odd angle. At the time the OTP investigators were there in 2001 the body of the minaret was still lying next to the mosque. By the time I was there a year later, it had been moved in preparation for reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, as to how the damage occurred, I'd refer you to the evidence of Witness Pazic at transcript page 605 and I'd also refer you to adjudicated facts 817 and 819. If we could go to the next slide. In 65 ter 28816 this formatted record starts at page 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what we are seeing here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a building I would include in my almost destroyed category. Almost destroyed means that the building is damaged beyond repair, but there are still identifiable elements above ground. You can see here that three of the four walls of the mosque had been completely blown-out and that a roof slab made of reinforced concrete has simply collapsed on to the body of the mosque. At the left you can see the minaret has been blown up as well, so the building is a total loss but it has not been cleared away so I couldn't -- wouldn't call it fully destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd refer you to the evidence of RM15 and adjudicated facts 1192 and 93. I'd ask that we turn to the next slide. The formatted record for this begins on page 213 of 65 ter 28816.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque in the village of Ahatovici. It's about 6 kilometres from Sarajevo in the Novi Grad municipality. It belongs in the almost destroyed category simply by virtue of the fact that it still has a few identifiable elements, the massive stump of the minaret and next to it upside down is the "serefe" or the balcony of the minaret where the muezzin used to come out. On the other side of the site there is -- there are also scattered other building elements, but basically the building is almost destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd refer Your Honours to adjudicated fact 1231 and ask that we turn to the next slide in 65 ter 28816 this entry begins on page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the mosque in the village of Atmacici and this illustrates the fact, simply, that if something was a border-line case between totally destroyed and almost destroyed or heavily damaged or lightly damaged, I tried to be conservative about it and always assign it to the higher category. You can see part of a lintel and to the right of the rubble is the stump of the minaret, but the mosque with very few modification could have fallen into the next damage category.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say the higher category?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Meaning -- I'm sorry, what I meant was if there was a choice between calling it totally destroyed and almost destroyed, if it was a border-line case I would make it the lighter degree of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd refer Your Honours to adjudicated fact 517 and ask that we turn to the next slide. And this formatted record starts on page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you help orient us a little bit for the two pictures next to each other, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The photo at left is from a book en masse published in 1990, so just two years before the war. If Your Honours look very closely, you will see that the picture is taken from a road which runs in front of the mosque, and at the right-hand side of the mosque between the fence that runs along the road and the mosque itself is a tall Bosnian Muslim tombstone. The photo at the right is one that I took in my 2002 fieldwork. You can see the same road running on the left-hand side of the photo. The same tombstone standing next to the road and next to the fence, and you can see very clearly on this one how you can tell the foundations, where they had been. So basically it's a 90-degrees-revolved picture. Imagine you're looking at the pre-war and you move 90 degrees counter clockwise and you get the photo on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we discussed earlier some of the comments that you cited in your report regarding the effect of what happened to a mosque on the community that worshipped there. Were you aware of any similar comments made about mosques in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and this was included in some of my prior reports for the Tribunal. In August of 1992 Simo Drljaca, who was the police chief for Prijedor and the five municipalities in Bosanska Krajina, was interviewed by Chuck Sudetic for the New York Times and Mr. Drljaca is reported to have said: With their mosques it's not enough to break the minaret. You have to shake-up the foundation because then they cannot build a new one. You do that and they will want to leave, meaning the Muslims. They will leave on their own, and that's more or less the quote as I have it from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For this site, Your Honour, I'd refer you to the evidence of, inter alia, RM080 and Exhibit P485. And I'd ask that we turn to the next slide. The formatted record for this site begins at page 38 of 65 ter 28816.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The photo at left -- this is the -- first of all, this is the parish church of St. Joseph in Prijedor, the only Catholic parish church in town. The photo at left was taken by the photo journalist Andreas Kaiser in September of 1992. The church had been destroyed by an explosion. The woman in front is collecting firewood and the only parts of the church that remain is -- are the large arch which stood between the altar and the congregation on the interior of the church. And not visible in the photo but known to me from an interview with the parish priest is that the church steeple -- a modern one was lying at an angle in the front. The photo at right was taken in the summer of 1995 after the church had been blown up a second time. If Your Honours will look carefully to the right of the tree at right, meaning near the right edge, you can see part of the arch. You can see it's broken off, but the rest of the building is simply gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: So this shows destructioning in stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is that next to what looks like part of a wall?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. It's next -- next to the group of trees in the background there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For this site I'd refer Your Honours to the evidence of RM57 and adjudicated fact 1103 and I'd ask that we turn to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This begins on page 180 of the formatted records.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, and this is the parish -- Catholic parish church in Kljuc, the church of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Again I will ask Your Honours to take a careful look at it. The road that is in both pictures is a little bit deceptive because the two photos are actually taken from opposite ends of the road. So on the picture at left the church is to the left of the road. The picture at right, the pile of stones that marks where the church stood is to the right of the road. The building to the left of the church in the pre-destruction photo can be seen behind a tree on the right-hand side of the post-destruction photo. The pre-destruction photo came from the Catholic church authorities. The post-destruction photo was taken by the Council of Europe survey team which went to Bosnia two years after the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then there are three remaining sites I think that you wanted to point us to and I would like to go through those quickly, but if we could go to the next slide this will be the Pudin Han-Velagici mosque starting on page 162 of the formatted records. Is this a site you visited yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a site I visited myself. At the time I was there it was under reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this picture we see a date, February 1993. What stage of -- what damage level would you say is reflected here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I would call this almost destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then if we could turn to the next slide, please. What do we see here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: And this is the same building which has again undergone a second phase of destruction. Only one of the little domes is left. The rest is a field of rubble and the imam's house behind is completely gone. This is another Council of Europe shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do the stages of destruction of a site like this allow you to draw any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion is that whoever did this wanted it to be gone, so they weren't satisfied with the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd refer Your Honours to adjudicated fact 762 and the evidence of RM18 and ask that we turn to the next slide beginning on page 218.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this also a site you visited yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a site I visited myself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. It's the market mosque in the centre of Srebrenica. This particular photo is a composite from the Zoran Petrovic Pirocanac video which is how we have the date. In the video the camera pans upward and so this was taken by adding together the various frames. I would draw Your Honours' attention to the three small square windows at the bottom which you will see in subsequent pictures as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would ask that we turn to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is taken a few days later, on the 19th of July, by the Serbian photo journalist, Mr. Djordje Vukoja, who visited Srebrenica that day. He was told that he had arrived just after the minaret had been blown up and he saw sappers laying the explosives for destroying the mosque itself. They told him to get out of there. He took the photo clandestinely from the car. You can see scattered stone work, the destroyed minaret at left. At right you can see one of the other Srebrenica mosques, the so-called white mosque, its minaret still intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What happened to that mosque, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That mosque was almost destroyed sometime between this and the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, would you mind to take me back one --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- page where the composite -- I just wanted to have another look at it. That is the photograph where the stills from the video --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've one question. In this composite photograph consisting of various shots from the video, the mosque is not damaged yet in any way at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In no way at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we see only one side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have other photographs in the formatted entry for this mosque that were taken by DutchBat before the fall of the town and the mosque was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next slide and the one after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what do we see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- can we see the other one just before this one. You said what happened to that mosque so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would just like to clarify, which mosque? The mosque with the minaret which was still intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the white mosque. It's the oldest mosque in Srebrenica. The market mosque is the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that white mosque was also destroyed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was destroyed after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What do we see here, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: On the left is a photograph taken by an Amnesty International team which came visiting Srebrenica in March of 1996. You can see the blasted minaret, again with that characteristic pattern of spreading out, indicating that there was a blast within. And the three square windows which were in the basement of the building, and you can see the building is simply gone, it used to be several storeys high. And the roof has landed on top of the foundation. And at right is a photo I took during my visit in July of 2002. The site is empty. You can see the same building in the background and the ritual deposit of garbage at the site, which is now overgrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Why do you call that a ritual deposit of garbage, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Because we are in the centre of Srebrenica, in the main market square, and the garbage is at the site of the mosque. It doesn't strike me as a logical place for a town dump.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, would you mind to take me back to the previous one as well. I have the problem that I can't switch from one page to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as to compare again. Let me see, yes. And the previous one. Could we now go forward again. And the last one again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it would assist, Your Honour, the formatted entry has additional photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was that deposit of rubbish at the site that you were mentioning, was that something you often saw at a site where a mosque used to be?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Very often, and I have a list of examples in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then I'd turn to the last example, the mosque in Novoseoci, the formatted record begins on page 130. Can you describe for us what we see on the left and right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: On the left what you see is a copy of the invitation to the dedication of the mosque which was built in 1990 in place of a mosque that had been destroyed in World War II. At right is a photo of the site after the war. You can see there it's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you describe this as rubble of the Novoseoci mosque. Can you describe for the Bench what your -- what you see in this picture that you can identify as part of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
